title: Scripture’s own gates and camps
source_text: Εἰ δέ τις βούλοιτο μὴ ἀφ᾿ ἧς παρέθετο αἱρέσεως ἀσημοτάτης ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ βιβλίων πῇ μὲν Ἰουδαϊκῶν καὶ ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς αὐτῶν ἀναγινωσκομένων, ἅπερ Χριστιανοὶ προσίενται, πῇ δὲ Χριστιανῶν μόνων λαβεῖν ἀφορμὰς τῆς μυστικωτέρας περὶ εἰσόδου ψυχῶν εἰς τὰ θεῖα θεωρίας, ἀναγνώτω τὰ ἐπὶ τέλει τῆς τοῦ Ἰεζεκιὴλ προφητείας ἑωραμένα τῷ προφήτῃ, ἐν οἷς διάφοροι πύλαι καταγεγραμμέναι εἰσὶν, αἰνισσόμεναί τινα περὶ τῆς διαφόρου εἰσόδου τῶν θειοτέρων ψυχῶν ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα· ἀναγνώτω δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῆς Ἰωάννου Ἀποκαλύψεως τὰ περὶ τῆς πόλεως τοῦ θεοῦ Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐπουρανίον καὶ τῶν θεμελίων καὶ τῶν πυλῶν αὐτῆς. εἰ δὲ δύναται διὰ συμβόλων καὶ τὴν ὁδὸν δεδηλωμένην τῶν ὁδευσόντων ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα μαθεῖν, ἀναγνώτω τοὺς ἐπιγεγραμμένους Ἀριθμοὺς Μωϋσέως καὶ ζητησάτω τὸν δυνάμενον αὐτὸν μυσταγωγῆσαι ἐπὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν παρεμβολῶν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ ἀναγεγραμμένα, ποῖαι μὲν κατὰ τὰ ἀνατολικὰ τεταγμέναι εἰσὶ μέρη ὡς πρῶται, ποῖαι δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ κατὰ λίβα (ἢ) κατὰ νότον, καὶ τίνες αἱ κατὰ θάλασσαν, καὶ τίνες αἱ τελευταῖαι κατὰ βοῤῥᾶν. ὄψεται γὰρ θεωρήματα οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητα ἐν τοῖς τόποις οὐδ᾿, ὡς Κέλσος οἴεται, μωρῶν τινων ἀκροατῶν καὶ ἀνδραπόδων δεόμενα· διαλήψεται γὰρ, τίνες ἐν αὐτοῖς, καὶ (τίνα) τὰ περὶ τῆς φύσεως τῶν κατειλεγμένων ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀριθμῶν καὶ ἐφαρμοσθέντων ἑκάστῃ φυλῇ, περὶ ὧν νῦν ἡμῖν ἐκθέσθαι ἔδοξεν οὐκ εὔκαιρον εἶναι. ἴστω δὲ Κέλσος καὶ οἱ ἐντυγχάνοντες αὐτοῦ τῷ βιβλίῳ ὅτι οὐδαμοῦ τῶν γνησίων καὶ θείων πεπιστευμένων γραφῶν ἑπτὰ εἴρηνται οὐρανοί· οὔτ᾿ ἀπὸ Περσῶν ἢ Καβείρων λαβόντες ἡμῶν οἱ προφῆται λέγουσί τινα οὐδ᾿ οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀπόστολοι οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone should wish (βούλομαι) to take starting points (ἀφορμή) of the more mystical (μυστικώτερος) contemplation (θεωρία) about the entry (εἴσοδος) of souls (ψυχή) into divine things (τὰ θεῖα), not from the most obscure (ἀσημότατος) sect (αἵρεσις) which he set beside (παρατίθημι), but from books partly Jewish and read (ἀναγινώσκω) in their synagogues (συναγωγή), which Christians accept (προσίεμαι), partly of Christians alone: let him read the things seen (ὁράω) by the prophet at the end of the prophecy of Ezekiel, in which different (διάφορος) gates (πύλη) are recorded (καταγράφω), hinting (αἰνίσσομαι) at something about the different entry of the more divine souls to the better things (τὰ κρείττονα); let him read also from the Apocalypse (ἀποκάλυψις) of John the things about the city of God, heavenly (ἐπουράνιος) Jerusalem, and its foundations (θεμέλιος) and its gates. And if he is able to learn also the way (ὁδός) shown (δηλόω) through symbols (σύμβολον) of those who will travel (ὁδεύω) to divine things, let him read the (books) entitled Numbers (Ἀριθμοί) of Moses, and let him seek the one able to initiate (μυσταγωγέω) him into what is recorded about the camps (παρεμβολή) of the sons of Israel: which are arrayed (τάσσω) toward the eastern (ἀνατολικός) parts as first, which toward the southwest (λίψ) or south (νότος), and which toward the sea (θάλασσα), and which are the last (τελευταῖος) toward the north (βορρᾶς). For he will see contemplations (θεώρημα) not easily despised (εὐκαταφρόνητος) in the passages (τόποι), nor, as Celsus thinks, needing (δέομαι) some foolish (μωρός) hearers and slaves (ἀνδράποδον); for he will distinguish (διαλαμβάνω) who are in them, and what concerns the nature of the numbers listed in them and fitted (ἐφαρμόζω) to each tribe (φυλή), about which it seemed to us not timely (εὔκαιρος) to set out now. Let Celsus and those who read his book know that nowhere in the genuine (γνήσιος) and divine Scriptures believed (πιστεύω, perf. pass.) are seven heavens (οὐρανοί) spoken of; nor do our prophets say anything taking it from Persians or Cabiri (Κάβειροι), nor the apostles of Jesus, nor the Son of God himself.
pass_b_english: But suppose someone wished to find starting points for a more mystical contemplation of how souls enter into divine things, not in the very obscure sect that he cited, but in books partly Jewish, read in their synagogues and accepted by Christians as well, and partly belonging to Christians alone. Let him read the visions seen by the prophet at the end of the prophecy of Ezekiel, in which different gates are described, hinting at something about the different ways in which more divine souls enter upon better things (Ezekiel 40–48). Let him read also, in the Revelation of John, what is said about the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and about its foundations and its gates (Revelation 21:2, 10–21; compare Hebrews 12:22).

And if he is able to learn also the way, shown through symbols, of those who will journey to divine things, let him read the book of Moses entitled Numbers, and let him look for someone able to initiate him into what is written there about the camps of the sons of Israel (Numbers 2:1–31): which are drawn up on the east side as first, which toward the southwest or the south, which toward the sea, and which are last, toward the north. For he will see in these passages contemplations not to be despised, and not, as Celsus supposes, such as need foolish hearers and slaves; for he will discern who are in them, and what concerns the nature of the numbers listed in them and assigned to each tribe; but we did not think it timely to set these things out now.

Let Celsus, and those who read his book, know that nowhere in the Scriptures received as genuine and divine are seven heavens spoken of. Nor do our prophets say anything they have taken from the Persians or the Cabiri; nor do the apostles of Jesus; nor does the Son of God himself.

choices.choice: ‘The very obscure sect that he cited’ (ἀφ᾿ ἧς παρέθετο αἱρέσεως ἀσημοτάτης): Origen looks back to what Celsus drew from the Mithraic material in 6.22 and forward to the Ophite diagram (6.24, same phrase ἀσημοτάτης αἱρέσεως); kept literal. Ezekiel 40–48 cited as a block because Origen names only ‘the end of the prophecy’ with its gates (e.g. 40:6–35; 48:30–35). ‘City of God, heavenly Jerusalem’ matches the wording of Hebrews 12:22 (πόλει θεοῦ ζῶντος, Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἐπουρανίῳ), so Hebrews is cited with ‘compare’; the foundations and gates are Revelation 21:14, 19–21. Numbers 2: east 2:3, south (LXX πρὸς λίβα) 2:10, sea/west 2:18, north 2:25, last to set out 2:31; Koetschau supplies (ἢ) before κατὰ νότον and (τίνα) in ‘what concerns the nature of the numbers’. ‘Toward the sea’ is kept as Origen (and the LXX) has it, meaning the west. ‘Genuine’ (γνησίων) contrasts with non-canonical writings that do speak of seven heavens; Origen names none here. Cabiri: Celsus had linked the seven heavens to Persian and Cabiric lore (6.22).
restored the dropped 'for' (γάρ) before 'he will discern', joining it to the sentence it explains
